utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are present. The presentation is exactly as it was yesterday. I needn't repeat it. Good morning to you, Professor. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'm glad to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic promised to finish within the next 15 minutes. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I didn't quite catch the last comment, but I'll try my best, Your Honour. I recognise the time estimates. It's just been going a little slow. We'll try to move as quickly as possible. The good news is my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecution indicated he may reduce his, although he's obviously still contemplating that and he said by almost 50 percent, but we'll see what happens, so we're still on schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to turn to the intercept on the 16th of July, 1995, at 1111 hours, if we may, and for the record the one we'd like to look at is P1187B, as in boy, and P1187A, which is the English version. Professor, I think it's found on the B/C/S version of your report at page 20. And just to quickly move along, I think this is the intercept that the word "triage" is mentioned, and I have a couple of questions in connection with this intercept. You had an opportunity to review it, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the alleged intercept of the conversation that took place on the 16th of July at 1111, and here there's practically nothing based on which one could undertake a linguistical analysis. There are only a dozen words here, and they are not pertinent at all. I mentioned them in my report, and let's not waste any more time. There's no body of language that would lend itself to any analysis, and as for the word "triage," I have explained that word in my analysis; i.e., I have transformed the analysis or the explanation from the relevant literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just if I may, I'd like to show the Court also in connection with the definition of "triage" Exhibit 2D583. If that can be brought up to the screen. I believe it's from a military encyclopedia as indicated defining the word "triage." Let me know when you see that, Professor, and I have a hard copy for you if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that what you relied on in order to draw your definition of what "triage" means, among other things?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your experience in giving lectures and in sitting in lectures, have you come across the use of "triage" by various colleagues or some colleagues in your area of expertise from time to time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For 25 years I was the first associate of Pavle Ivic, a member of the academy of sciences. He was the editor in chief of a magazine, and I was his second in command or his secretary. When a contribution arrived featuring unimportant data, irrelevant information that might burden the text on it necessarily, the professor would usually say, and I quote: "This has to be triaged. Slobodan, you are in for some triage work." And when it so happened that a contribution contained dubious data or data of dubious value that had to be eliminated, the professor would say, and I quote again: "This has to be triaged now, and if we don't get around to it the interested reader always does his or her own triage." In other words, a selection or sifting of what is important from what is not important and things like that. A month ago at a session of the department for literature and art of the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Republika Srpska, there was a discussion about the procedure that would follow surrounding the election of new members of the academy. The procedure envisages that all the proposals should be referred to the academy, and the academy then submits these proposals to the competent departments or sectors for evaluation, and the evaluation concerns the quality of the proposed candidates, which has to be documented by written papers. At the session, Rajko Petrov Nogo, a member of the academy, Rajko Petrov Nogo, a prominent poet, summed up our task by the following words: "All the material arrives here, and we will carry out a triage." I have noted the word word-for-word because I knew I would needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the context of this case you may or may not be familiar that the Prosecution has taken a view as to what the word "triage" means, but for our purposes, and I know you may not know this factually as to what was happening in July -- or on July 16th, 1995, but to assist us as to what may have been going on in connection with this word "triage" at 1111, let's look at another intercept of the same date, 16th of July, 1995, and that's P1200D and P1200A. If we could please have that up on the screen. And this seems -- as it's coming up seems to be a conversation between two individuals, Djurdjic and a female by the name of Jelena, and Professor, you had an opportunity to review this intercept, and I am going to ask you just a couple of questions in connection with this. This intercept involves a situation that -- or a discussion involving Potocari and Bratunac and the fact that there's 59 individuals and then perhaps even 46 in another place that may have been wounded. Now, in this intercept did these two individuals -- I know it doesn't necessarily relate or identify or compromise Mr. Beara, but these two individuals Djurdjic and Jelena, do they talk about the word "selection" and/or "triage"? I'm pressed for time, so I'm sorry for having to go this quickly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it. The text has been shown to me, and mutatis mutandis, this is it. This is the same semantics. This is the same meaning that you can find in literature and that I found to have the meaning that we encounter in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Great, if you could be kind enough, with the Court's permission and the usher's assistance, if we can have you circle where the word "triage" or "selection" appear, but just to maybe go a little faster I'll just direct you. Both words appear and they're on the second half of the paper, and for the Court and others who are watching, if we could turn to the second page of P1200D, and at the top of that page I believe -- I'm sorry, P1200A, the English version, the second page of that document on the first sentence is where the words seem to appear. Do you see it in the B/C/S version, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Seven lines from the bottom. Now it's in the middle of the screen now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it now, but I don't have a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: She will assist you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Please pencil. Pencil. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Both words appear correct, Mr. Remetic, both the words "triage" and "selection," correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help me with this. Do you see immediately above that that they are discussing the situation in Bratunac and Potocari and they're using the numbers of 59 individuals and 46 individuals among other estimates that they're providing with respect to the wounded and/or injured. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. And if you're asking me -- are you asking me what I understand when I see the words "selection" and "triage"? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this probably means that healthy people should be selected from the sick people or something like that. That means that they have to be separated, selected; that would be a triage, a selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it also says here that a selection should be made as to who would go to Belgrade, who would go to Tuzla, or maybe everybody would go to Tuzla. In any case, this is a selection according to some criteria. This is by no means a frontal approach, a blanket approach; and this is what is expected, as a matter of fact, when you see the word "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, under any -- under any circumstance as a linguist and a dialectologist can you assume that these people were being selected and being transferred for either triage or treatment in medical facilities, or can anyone under any reasonable circumstance have the word "triage" be interpreted to mean "execution"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's objectionable, Your Honour. That relates to the province of the Court to determine the facts in the case, and I think it's an inappropriate question to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't even think the objection is sound, and I think we have a linguist here, and I think the Prosecution on its own has decided to give definitions to words and taking them without looking at the complete picture as we have with this intercept, and I think if a linguist can't give a reasonable definition, who can? It's not a legal term that the Court with all due respect should define, but the Court should look at what inferences it may draw from certain facts. If it's a fact that triage was used, we can -- should be allowed to bring expert or even lay evidence to define it. I truly believe that the objection is not sound and has no merit at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The objection in particular, Your Honour, is to the part of the question that my colleague puts to this witness where he asks whether anybody can under any reasonable circumstance have the word "triage" be interpreted to mean "execution." That's a question of fact. That's not a question of expertise and opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Vanderpuye, at the end of the day what you have juxtaposed here is the interlocutors, alleged interlocutors that intercept who used the word "triage," and in that context it's us and not the witness who is going to decide what they meant when they were using the word "triage" and an expert who has already given us his explanation of the word "triage." You can proceed with the question if you like, but do you think it's going to take you anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, given the Court's comments -- I was hoping it would, but given the Court's comments it seems unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking again at the exhibit of the 16th of July, 1995, P1187A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we can, Mr. President, please save the document in which the witness has circled in the B/C/S the word "selection" and "triage," which was the prior intercept that was just shown it him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, look at the screen when they get it up, and it will be again P1187A, which is the English version, and P1187B, which is the manuscript handwritten version of the intercept where this word "triage" shows you. We talked about it briefly, and you told us that there was a limited and insufficient linguistics corpus which respect to the words that may be attributed purportedly to Mr. Beara, but I'd like for you to help me with this, and I could do it, but since you're here. Who uses the word "triage"? Is it the gentleman with the initial that they use for C, Cerovic, is it X, or is it the person that they purport is the initial B for Beara? So when the Court looks at it, they'll see what this individual who used the word may mean by the word "triage." Who uses it? Look at the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you can see it very well. Cerovic is the one who is using that, a person under C.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Look down five sentences. He uses it for a second time. The word "triage" appears. Again, it's under whose initial?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where lower down?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Four lines down, you see the initial C, the first one, then X, then C again, then the letter X where the word is used. Do you see it? It's the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16th.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I practically know all the texts by heart. Yes. Please, there is only one mention by Cerovic of triage here; underneath, there is no mention of the word "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you with that. I don't know that you have the right document in front of you, Professor. Help me -- just look at the screen with me. If you seen on the very first line, the first -- you know, it says -- an introduction says triage. Then if you go on the left side, if you count with me X, C, X, again under the person who is X who is an unknown, the word "triage" appears, right, for the second time? Do you see that? And then --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. Yes. The word "triage" appears on this page three times, first under C --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you, Professor. Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then X.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Actually, it appears four times, but let me walk you through it, okay, so that we see who actually uses "triage." It's used the first time by Cerovic, then by the gentleman who is known as X. Immediately before that it's used by whom again? Do you see it? The very next line, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: X. A triage would be carried out. That's X.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then immediately --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: C, to carry out the triage of the captives. [In English] Cerovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then if you look five lines from the bottom, again, under the initial C for Cerovic, do you see whether or not he uses the word "triage"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C, again, to carry out a triage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's four times; three times by Cerovic, once by X. Do you see ever the initial or the person who they attribute the initial B to be Beara ever utilizing the word "triage" in this or any other intercept that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to another topic in the interest of time. Sir, when I say the word "govorim," that means to speak, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know it's hard to do this because you are getting the translation, but I have to do it or would like to do it for the benefit of my learned friends and the Court. Let's turn to the intercept of July 13th, 1995, at 1009, please, and that's P01130B. And that's the B/C/S version, which they'll bring up for you, and the English version of this intercept is P01130E, as in "evening." Now, I got the short version of this intercept here, and if we could just go to the page, although -- yeah, let's stick with this. And Professor, I know you have a limited knowledge of English, and I'm going to help you here, and I'm sure the Court won't mind nor will my learned friends, but if you look at the left-hand side and you see the English version of the text, after the initial B the second word says "speaking," So it's if I were to say if I answered the phone "Ostojic govori," or "Ostojic speaking," that's what that would denote, would it not? See at the very second word after the initial B. I think there's even an arrow or --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you help me with this, sir, because this is a translation supposedly of the very manuscript and/or typed text that they had presented to the Court as evidence. Can you look at that first page and tell me if the word "speaking" appears anywhere after Beara's name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that it's put like that anywhere. I did not understand or treat this transcript in that manner, that is to say, as an introduction of Beara by his last name, his personal introduction. As I understand it, this "Beara" was written by hand of the -- by the operator. That is the identification that he had made of the speaker whom he had allegedly taped.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that in your opinion on that. I'm just curious to know if you see, because my B/C/S is obviously never going to be as good as yours, if you see the word "speaking" or "govori" on that intercept on that very first page, and I have a couple more, so stay with me just on the word "speaking" if you don't mind. We don't see it on that page. If we could have the court officer or usher on e-court please flip to the third page of this document P01130, which has the ERN ending in 810. Now, for some reason that intercept --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is Beara. Yes, I've it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, hold on. For some reason, and the Court's heard evidence of this, the intercept operator crossed this section out and then rewrote it, and then our learned friends from the Prosecution were kind enough to translate it for us, and we have that translation. Actually, we have two versions. We'll talk about the second version in a minute, but let's stick with this version. If you see this new and I guess improved intercept manuscript that the operator created, does it say anywhere after the word "Beara" on that first line that he's actually speaking? Does it say "Beara govorim" as reflected in this translation that the Prosecution offered to the Court? Do you see the word there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no word "speaking," and these two versions are different at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we'll get to your opinion --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to break it down as -- and try to get through this as painlessly as possible. If we can have the court please bring up P1130A, which is a second translation of this document, please, and it has the ERN number 00912596. And I know you can't read the Prosecution's mind and I'm sure they'll explain it to us, but let me ask it anyway. How do you think that they came up with this added -- or these added words that Beara is speaking when in fact nowhere in either the crossed-out version of the written manuscript or in the newer written manuscript does that word appear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question is inappropriately placed to this witness, and my colleague is fully aware of the translation process that the Prosecution has to go through in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Move to your next ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I need to stick with this for a minute, but I have to respond, and I'm fully aware of as they are of my duties of what their duty are to this Court to bring revised changes and updated translations if they see it, not to stick with an old translation whether or not it was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in any event, sir, look at the second translation that the Prosecution has, and I know you are limited in your English. It also has the words "Beara speaking." Do you see that on the very first line? Sir, look at the screen please. Professor? Professor? Professor? Look at the screen --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, but there is no word "speaking" in the manuscript, and this is crucial for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good enough. And that's why, sir, in your table, if you look at this document, you put a negative on that first intercept that you reviewed of the 13th of July, 1009 hundred hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Knowing that you've told us that the speech model and the speech pattern of Mr. Beara having listened to him for seven, eight hours in April, having listened to the tape of four years ago that we just recently received, were you able to discern any of the Cakavian or Ekavian dialect in this intercept here, or just give us your opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty as to whether or not you are able to determine whether this intercept can be attributed to Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot attribute it to him, and it is my professional duty not to do so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why can you not, because there was a lack of characteristics, linguistically and dialectically speaking?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are not sufficient elements on the basis of which I could do that. There are insufficient elements. His today's way of speaking from the way he spoke in April, there is almost nothing left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll look at your report for further clarification on that. Now, we were going to go through some of the other intercepts, and we do have time, I hope. But just quickly, the intercept of the 13th of July at 1919, although though you looked at it because of the name "Ljubisa" appears on it, I think it's pretty fair and I'm sure my learned friends will agree, they're not attributing this intercept to Mr. Beara at all, so let's not even spend too much time on that, right? Professor? Oh. And then if you look at the intercept --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at the next intercept that we have, which is 13th of July, 1995, at 1945 hours, that intercept, also, is one that the OTP is not attributing to Mr. Beara, and that's why we're just going to skip it here and let them explain it to the Court, if necessary, even though there the name "Ljubisa" appears, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then just going down our little list here --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. There's the name "Ljubo" that appears here, but I think this is Borovcanin [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think, Professor, and in all fairness, if you look at the intercept at 1945 hours on the 13th of July, which is P1148 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologize to my learned colleague. I have just one -- I just noticed in the transcript. I believe that the witness said "but they say it's Borovcanin," and here it says "I think this is Borovcanin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for the correction. Do you agree with that because I don't speak the language, so I can't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's more than fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why I was going to come back to it just to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But just -- I have to clarify one thing the name says "Ljubisa" on that intercept, sir, and you said in the transcript, I think, that it says "Ljubo," but if you look at the intercept of 1945 hundred hours it says "Ljubisa" on at least three occasions, does it not? Why don't we bring up P1148, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't hear the answer that the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The witness, I believe, did not provide an answer yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ljubisa is mentioned, but there is no basis to establish a connection with Mr. Beara. The OTP themselves reached a conclusion that this was Ljubisa, Ljubomir, Ljubo Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me look at the next exhibit with you, Professor, which is - I know we are going fast - the 13th of July, 1995, at 2305 hours, which is P1153A and B, A for the English and B for the B/C/S. This intercept -- and now, we've been talking about the intercepts of the 13th, and we've seen, obviously, one that you think is not relevant, one that had inadequate corpus, one that -- the issue with speaking, the other one that the Prosecution has defined who the individual is other than Mr. Beara. Then let's look at this last intercept on that date, the 13th, 2305. You let me know when you've had an opportunity to look at that, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is also an intercept between two individuals, one individual whose name appears as "Ljubo," correct? You see that on the third line of the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we brought in evidence or we have tried to that it's a different individual. I think the Prosecution - in fact, I know they have they have - they've conceded that it's not Mr. Beara on this intercept. We have this intercept here for you to review because the name "Ljubo" or derivative of his name "Ljubisa" appeared. Sir, looking at this, do you know how many different derivatives of the name "Ljubisa" exists in the B/C/S language or in the Serbo-Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to address my friend's comments, that is the position of Prosecution that is not Mr. Beara. That is not the Prosecution's position. The Prosecution's position is uncertain as to whether or not it's Mr. Beara. I just want to the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's more correct, Mr. Ostojic, from what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From what I remember, it was pretty clear that my learned friend Mr. McCloskey conceded the point that it Ljubo Sobot because it was a Zvornik brigade logbook that clearly showed on this specific date there was a discussion involving food supplies, but we can address that at a later time. I'm sure we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But anyway, Professor, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye is correct, Mr. President, just so that it's -- we just can finish this right now. Mr. Vanderpuye is correct. We're not sure who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor Remetic, when looking at this, is this conversation a monologue or a dialogue between two individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's hard to answer yes when I gave you both options, but I like that, but which one is it? You think the operator captured both sides of the conversation or one side of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the purpose of a linguistic analysis, there are no facts here because according to the operator's words, this is a monologue of General Mladic because his interlocutor, Osertin [phoen] Ljubo, as it is mentioned here, was -- could not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you about the name "Ljubo." Is it a common name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo is a very common name among Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how many -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It usually denotes an abbreviated version of a name, a hypochoristic, that's a pet name for a term of endearment, a shortened version of the full name such as Ljubisav, Ljubisa, Ljubodrag, Ljubomir. The glossary of the Serbian names compiled three decades ago contains 47 versions, the basis of which is "Ljub," and of all these names "Ljubo" can be one of the hypochoristics, or Ljuba.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and I don't know if you identified -- I know you gave us several examples. How about Ljubko? Do you think that might -- or do you know if Ljubko, that came can be shortened to be Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Ljubinko and Ljubko and Ljupce and Ljuboda can all be that. There's also one very important thing pertaining to this case, the Serbian names, the meanings of which imply something nice or pleasant or dear, Ljub and the similar, can be given as secondary names to the people having any other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from my own environment that Ljuba, Mile, Mico, and their proper first names were Nikola, Petar, Ostoja, Slobodan, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me go a little more specific with you, and I know we're talking about general and the various number of possibilities that it could be Ljubo, but let's look specifically in the area of where the events were unfolding. And we heard from witnesses whose names do begin with Ljubo or Ljuban or Ljubko or Ljubomir already, but let's look at Exhibit 2D592, and if you could just tell me briefly, and I know you're not a military expert, Professor, but I think this document essentially speaks for itself and I thinks is a -- it's from the command of the 33rd Motorised Brigade, and it is from 1996, but I think from that you can look -- and the name appears, if you look at that little list of individuals who was there, almost on the first three lines you see two people whose names are identified by the name of Ljubo and Ljubislav, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's try to go closer to the events of when they were unfolding with respect to this case, July of 1995. Can we have 2D593, please, and I believe this is a list of officers for the month of July in 2000 -- I mean, July 1995. Now, we've seen this document before with other witnesses, so it's -- if you look down, just take a look quickly if you scroll down the names here, and you tell me if you see -- like, for example, in number 9, do you see anything that would be a derivative or actually the name "Ljubo" under that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Colonel Ljubo Sobot here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to know what his rank was as well. If we scroll down it look at the 13th line, and it has another Ljubo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lieutenant Colonel Ljubo Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a list of July of 1995. There's a colonel there called Ljubo, there's a lieutenant-colonel called Ljubo, and we have other lists with approximately 17 different names of individuals who are on there. Could any one of those individuals have been people on an intercept, and if you had heard the tape recordings it would have assisted you, would it not, in determining who -- to whom to attribute these conversations? Is that reasonable and fair, do you think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question calls for speculation as to whether or not this witness has a basis of knowledge as to who could be and who couldn't be on an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no comments to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you should move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, from the analysis and the materials that you provided, did the Prosecution give you any alternative names or individuals whose names appear or could be derived from the word "Ljubo" or "Ljubisa" or "Ljubomir" or "Ljubislav" or "Ljubko" or "Ljuban"? Did they provide any such information on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me, I don't know. To me as a linguist, every Serbian name can in practice among his family members be Ljubo, Mico, Dragan, and whatever. I'm speaking from my personal experience. This is my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, and just give the Court -- you mentioned Mica and other names. Mica is also often a common nickname for many different names, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it's -- is it as many as for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to go back to the transcript. Could "Mica" be spelled because the way "Mica" is spelled in the transcript is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You handle this, Mr. Ostojic, please, knowing both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, sir, that -- and we are going very fast, Professor, and I do apologise. It's entirely my fault. When you use the word "Mica" or "Mico," can you just be kind enough to spell it for us, please, and I think it's M-I-C-O and M-I-C-A, but why don't you help us here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M-I-C, with a diacritic, O.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, "Mica" would be the same way the diacritic only with an A as the last letter, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Give us a sampling just briefly of the names that could be utilized who used the name "Mica" as a nickname. What names -- we know from "Ljubisa" you can have "Ljubo" among other common first names, but just give me an example of "Mica," if you can.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an often-found hypochoristic derivative of the name Milorad, Milutin, Miroslav, Miladin, Milita, Milisa, Miljko, Milos, Milun, et cetera. However, Mico can also be a secondary name or a second same of a person who has been christened under a different name. A neighbour of mine had nine children, seven daughters, and the last born son was called Tadija. His family always only called him Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, how about just briefly, because it's relevant to the intercepts that we have, how about the nickname Zoka or Zoko? Is that also a common nickname for various other first names? Z-O-K-A.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know. I'm not an expert in onomastics. I don't particularly deal in the names. "Zoka" is a new nickname. It could be Zoka, or Zoki just like Miki.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next item, which is the 14th of July, 1995, the intercept, sir, at 2102 hours, which is 65 ter 1164, and we have it marked in e-court at P1164C for the English version, B for the manuscript. We'd like that one up, and then just so the Court knows, there's the E, which is the typed version. Professor, I'd like to ask you, you've obviously reviewed this; I've read your analysis and report in connection with this intercept, but can you tell me in a nutshell whether this intercept, sir, in your professional opinion can be attributed to Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this alleged intercept there's very little linguistic data. Some words may be linked with the name of Mr. Beara or are, indeed, linked with him. According to the operator's words, he does not know the code 155, which is quite odd for a high ranking officer not to be familiar with the unit. Furthermore, in the manuscript or in the handwritten version, we also have the admission of the operator that some errors and omissions have been made and that the identity has been mistaken. They subsequently added to the first letter B, the letter E, which is easily checked. It can be checked very easily, and by doing that they have denoted Beara, whereas it should have been the Badem station. It says here very nicely that the person at the switchboard is speaking, and they attributed these words to somebody else, and at the end there is a remark added by the hand of the operator through a mistake of the switchboard operator at Badem. We intercepted a conversation between the person X and the other person Y, but we could not actually hear that person while the conversation was being intercepted and while the line was open for Jokic 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Professor, and looking at this, I know from reading your report, and you correct me if I'm wrong, that the linguistics corpus of this intercept was insufficient in order to determine whether you can attribute that to Mr. Beara. I know you've highlighted other problems with this intercept, and the Court has looked at that. I do have one other question in connection with this witness and we have heard -- or this intercept. Now, yesterday I asked you, I believe, at page 40 approximately regarding the word "phonology," and it was certainly my mistake, and you told me that phonology was -- and help me distinguish phonology from phonetics. There's obviously a distinction, but help me understand phonology versus phonetics.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Phonetics is a science that deals with the physical acoustic properties of sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know you told us yesterday that from reviewing the statements from the various operators they were not required to record or capture these conversations from a phonological standpoint, but now let me ask you from a phonetic -- or phonetically speaking, do you remember reading statements and testimony from these witnesses where they have said that they phonetically were told to capture the conversations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that they had been told to register that. Those people are foreigners to linguistic terminology. Linguistic terminology is something foreign to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me now -- and I know we have another intercept left with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I would be asking for additional time given the recent or at least a month ago tendering of audio recordings. I know we've mentioned the one that was in the Prosecution's possession since the 11th of October, 2004. We just received that on the 18th of July, 2008. Also, we had a couple of other recordings that we have shown to Professor Remetic that I'd like for him to comment on with the Court's permission, and they just came up because of the filing on the 18th of July -- not filing but discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection on your part? We have already gone beyond the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that you had requested quite considerably, I would say. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have no material objection to it, but I would like to point out that the interview a relatively short document, and I think it was simply asked whether he would like to be interviewed and he declined, and that's the extent of that audio material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I guess that's basis for not producing it to us under the rules, but I don't accept that. But let me move on in the next few minutes, if I may. If we can 2D566, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, we looked at Ljubisa Beara as you interviewed him in 2008, and we saw some of his short interview, I guess, that the Prosecution took in 2004. But I want to know if we saw a transcript with Mr. Beara just identifying this one because I just don't have the time to walk you through it all linguistically, but I will probably apply to have you come back and look at these audio recordings. And if you look at 2D556, sir, I want you just to turn to the second page, and this is a conversation that purports to have occurred on the 6th of June, 1995, which is temporally closed if not within the parameters of the indictment that's been filed, and this is a conversation that is among several individuals including Ljubisa, or it says Ljubised Beara and Tolimir Zdravka, but it's Zdravko, and I just want to look at the second page of the B/C/S version there. And if you can look at the second line where Mr. Tolimir uses the word "nereseno." Do you see that? Maybe if we could enhance it or enlarge it that would help.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is not necessary. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look right underneath that, it seems to have a word -- almost the same word purportedly utilized by Mr. Beara. Is that the same word, or are those two different words, "nereseno" and "nerjeseno," with the J? Do you see it immediately underneath that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me what the difference is between the two words, the meaning first, if any?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no difference in the meaning. There can't be any meaning. This is just the way it is pronounced. The only difference is in the way these two words are pronounced. There is no difference in the meaning at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And one person from a different region would be using it with a certain dialect, and another person from a different region would be using a different dialect, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I understand it, but let me stick with it for just another minute or so. The one that's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The one that's attributed to Mr. Tolimir, can you tell us by looking at that word what -- strike that. Let's look at the one from Mr. Beara having interviewed -- or having been with him in 2008, listening to the audio of 2004 with the Prosecution. Now, looking at this in 1995, can you discern from this, sir, as to what region or which dialect Mr. Beara was speaking in 1995, June, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is insufficient. This is too little to lead to an unambiguous opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where it says "nerjeseno" here, I heard it as "nereseno," which is not surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here where it says "nerejeseno" under Ljubisa Beara, J is often lost after an R. It's very difficult to pronounce. The word "vrjema," if pronounced as "vrjeme," by somebody, V-R-J-E-M-E, very often this comes out as in true Ekavians, and that's something that we are aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you another quick transcript, and it's 2D587, and I -- sir, I know you haven't had ample time to review this, and I apologise for that because we recently received it and we've been gone for awhile here, but let -- I think you could help me with this. 2D587, and this, again, just as we're looking at it, purports to be a conversation of the 13th of August, 1995, between a person by the name of Brke or Brko and Ljubisa Beara, and what I'm going to do is just ask -- and I wanted you to look at the front page so you could see the date on the top, and then we'll ask if we can go to the second page of document, and they'll get there. And if they can please enlarge the centre of the document. If you could just scroll down a little. Sorry. Just on the record, there was just a mistake. The prior exhibit given, it's ERN number -- I mean, it's the P number, and that one the transcript reflects a different number. The one that we had just seen, not this one, was P -- 2D556. Just so the record is clear, and this one that we are looking at now is 2D587. And sir, sticking with this, I noticed in the middle of the page there, if you look at the language that's being attributed to Mr. Beara here, and it says -- there's -- in the middle of the page, "A Sta Se Dogoja." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A Sta Se Dogoja." With a J, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be consistent with which kind of dialect or from which region, if you can help me with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cakavian. This is a Split version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just look at almost towards the end of that page where it says "Dobro burazer." Do you see that? And if you could just read that whole sentence, and I really want you to focus on the third word from the end of that sentence, and then give me an opinion as to whether that is Cakavian or from Split or which dialect you may think it is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the sentence: "Very well, brother, I'll see about that. Probably I won't be able to do it either tomorrow or the day after." Is that what you mean? I suppose it's a literal word. This is a form found in people speaking Ekavian. If it was spoken from a person from Zagreb, it would probably be the najviro jatne [phoen]. However, in the speech practice you can hear it used in this form, and I suppose that this is used by the Bosnian Ekavian speakers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last exhibit, if I may, please, with 2D594, which is the brief interview that the officer of the Prosecution conducted with Mr. Beara without his lawyers on the 11th of October, 2004. And I know it's brief, and I know what the limitations are for having a brief corpus here, but I'd just like to -- and I know you looked at this briefly without having adequate time to fully analyse it. I want to just highlight a couple of the words that appear, and we pulled them out. If you could look on the third page of that document, sir, and thankfully this has the lines numbered, so we'd be able to follow one another quite quickly. And in the B/C/S version, I'm going to direct you to the third page, line 9. The word "razumem" means "understand," and Mr. Beara uses the word here as transcribed and as heard on the tape audio recording "razumim." Do you see that? Line 9, please. Oh, I'm sorry, on this copy -- that's odd --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says -- Yes, it says "razumim" in the 7th line. I apologize. I beg your pardon. This is good. Yes, it's well written. Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning that, just because I have it as line 9, so I apologise to the Court. My copy has line 9, but we'll check as to why there may be two different versions, so that's why -- I see that it's 7. Now, looking down, is that consistent, is that use of that word "razumim" as opposed to "razumem" or "razumijem," would that be consistent with the dialect that you heard Mr. Beara in 2008 and that we've seen, although briefly, from the use of the Split region and the Cakavian dialect that Mr. Beara utilized both in 1995 and 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to the audio recording, albeit in a haste. There are very few words here, very little linguistic material. The conversation took place in a very formal atmosphere in rather official circumstances. This was a statement provided to the OTP, and everybody who is in that situation uses a very standard language. They are not relaxed, and this form "razumim" is precisely something that reflects the way Mr. Beara spoke in April, and I remind you that I encountered "razumijem" in transcripts. I also encountered "razumem," but I never came across the form that I heard from Beara and that I heard on this audio recording. There is very little information, but in my view this is very important proof for me that I did my job as I should have done it, to avoid any false modesty. This is just a confirmation of that because I found this type of speech in Beara's words in April, and I've not come across any similar examples in the intercepted conversations that I perused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look just quickly -- and thank you. Let's just quickly look in the three minutes - and I'm grateful to the Court, I truly am for giving me that additional time - three lines down on line 12, I think it is, the word "lijepa" or "lijepa" as some would say. Do you see that? Is that distinctive for any region or dialect that you could look of? Lijepa, I think it's on line 12. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hvala lijepa and hvala lipa are both mostly connected with the western variant of the former common language and currently Croatian standard variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have one other topic that I just forgot to mention. I know it's in your report, and it's related to the 13th of July, 1995, intercept at 1009, Professor, and we did rush through it a little bit. You found -- and I apologise for leading on this. Did you find from the transcripts of the intercepted conversations any evidence of a Dalmatian speaking or someone with a Cakavian dialect such as that which we've seen from Mr. Beara in 1995, June and August respectfully, such as that we've seen in 2004 and 2008 respectfully, and I want to focus on the one word that I think Madam Frease was talking about, and that's the word "Sjor" on the July 13th, 1995, intercept, again, at 1009, and that's P01130B for the B/C/S version and the same number designated for the English version with the letter E as well as A. If the Court remembers there was two English versions, and that's where the beginning states Beara is speaking in the translation but not necessarily on the manuscript. So can you tell us what the word "sjor" means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from the Italian word "Signor." In the coastal dialects, this has become "sjor" or some such thing, so this would be a typical example of Cakavian, which appears only once. The words like "sjor," "gospon," "burazer" are commonly used as filler words in one's speech, and it is indicative that "sjor" does not repeat anywhere else. It doesn't appear in the conversations with Mr. Beara in April, either. In my view, this is really odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we have it, why don't you spell it for us in the transcript, although I could do it, I think. It's S-J-O-R with a diacritic over the S, but I think that's accurate, and it's reflected in the written form, as well, but I don't know if it was captured immediately. Go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, help me with this in the last minute we have. I'm looking at the last page of your report in English, page 30, second to the last paragraph. I just want to understand with respect to this word "sjor" and the context. You state in your report - and I apologise if I read it fast, but I'll try not to - "A comparison of the language of the alleged intercepts and Mr. Beara's current manner of speech has brought to the surface their diametric opposition. In the transcripts submitted to us, there is literally not one trait of the Split variant of Cakavian Ikavian, not one Cakavian morphological feature, while in the lexical domain only "sjor," again the S with the diacritic J-O-R --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, let us -- help find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 30 on the English version of his report, second to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: 31 in the English, page 31, second last --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologize. I have what was filed with the filing number on it, and I'm specifically looking at page 30, and it's the second to the last, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: It is the second to the last. It's just the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's the second to the last paragraph of the report, whatever page that may be, I guess. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, and it's soon break time --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And if I may just inquire, have we found it, Honourable Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying again, and I wanted to do this, and I tried to do it in the beginning. You talk about not one trait or -- and I think you explained, it the variant from the Cakavian Ikavian, not one Cakavian morphological feature, and then while in the lexical domain only "sjor" was registered. Is that where you found the word "sjor" on the July 13th, 1995, intercept at 1009 that we see in front of us here? Is that the one time you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only example, the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this last question before we go on break: Did you find with the exception of August 1st, 1995, the intercept that we discussed which is on your table at 1002 hours where you obviously placed a positive or plus sign in the four categories, did you find from your review of the intercept conversations that any of them can be attributed to Mr. Beara based upon a reasonable degree of linguistics certainty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find any foundation to attribute anything to him, and the closest possible example that may be linked to Mr. Beara's name is the third version of the same conversation, which I believe took place on the 15th of July at 10 o'clock. This is where we have three versions of the same conversation, or rather, we have three different versions of the same conversation which have been obtained in my opinion by the subsequent interventions and harmonisations of the three texts which had been recorded by three persons who probably hailed from different areas. This conversation, or rather, this transcript, or rather, the three transcripts took most of my time. I carried out a very detailed comparison in order to be able to observe linguistic differences. At the very beginning of the three transcripts, I noticed some discrepancies as well as the time differences, which I could not account for in any other way but this, which is also my final opinion: These were not three different conversations but just one, and that one conversation has appeared in three different versions, which have been polished subsequently, and the third version would be the closest to the way Beara speaks but not so close to allow me to attribute this version to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's probably overdue.

utterances.text: Yes, let's have the break now. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Given the Court's comments and your generosity in having me go further than the estimated time, yeah, we'll stop here and we'll let the Prosecution ask or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me now -- Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
