utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That throws the ball in your court, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you. Good morning to my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Remetic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution, I will put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination. I just want to let you know if there's anything that I ask you that is unclear or you don't understand, just let me know and I'll do my best to rephrase it in a way that we can both better understand one another. Now, you testified rather extensively concerning the development of dialects in the former Yugoslavia. You talked about the historical underpinnings as well as a contact between peoples and the exchange of language between them as concerns the development and acquisition of the dialects you are speaking about. But I want to focus you, if I may, on more practical aspects of your report. I noticed in your report that you referred to on page 17 certain terms that borrow from the romance languages, and you indicate that that is typically present in the sea coast areas where you've indicated Mr. Beara has spent a substantial amount of time. In particular, you say that words such as "sjor," "gospon," "burazer" and those types of terms occur frequently in everyday speech of the people that use them, and you said that while this is lacking in the transcripts you examined though you looked for them. Now, if I could, one of the intercepts that you looked at was one on July 13th at 1009, and if I could just have that up in e-court, please. That's 65 ter 1130. The B/C/S is 1130B, and I think that would be the best to look at just for now. All right. Now, if I could page forward to ERN the page number ending 815. Okay. And now, if you look at the words that are attributed to B counting up from the bottom, if you count to the third line where there is actually written words, you see the word "burazer." You see that on your screen, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just page back now to page number 813. Actually before we do that, just a moment. The phrase that is written there, if you could just read that out so we are all clear that we are talking about the same thing where you see it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Very well. Excellent. Now, listen to me, broth."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could go to page ending -- all right, it will be page 6, I'm told, this intercept. That should be ERN ending 814. All right. Just one more page back to 813, please. Thank you very much. This would be the second line that is attributable to B. Do you see the word "burazer" there, also, and if you could just read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Excellent, broth. Super."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if I could just page back to ERN ending 810. Okay. I think that's fine. Below the crossed-out part of the handwritten text, you see a reference to the word "sjor," as in Sjor Lucic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. "Hello, Sjor Lucic. How are you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, all of those words appear in that one intercept. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could refer you to intercept 11 -- 65 ter 1178. 1178B, I believe. Yeah, that's perfect. Thank you very much. Now, if you look five lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you can see attributable to B in that conversation a line that begins with "Tako." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. "Listen, broth."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's the same word that we just referred to on the previous intercept on 13 July, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record the intercept I'm referring to is 15 July 1995, 0954 hours. Now, Mr. Ostojic also introduced you to a number of other intercepted communications. This one is 3603, 65 ter 3603. All right. If we could just go to the second page, please. Just bear with me a moment because I have a slightly different pagination. All right. Just about the middle of the page on the page at the right, you can see what is attributed to Mr. Beara as the words "Dobro burazer." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Okay, broth. Mrki wants to speak to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could, I'd like to go to 65 ter 3607. Sorry, for the record 3603 is an intercept dated 6/6/1995 between Tolimir and Beara. 3607 is dated 05/12/1995 between Mrkovic and Beara. If I could - bear with me a moment so I can orient myself - if we could go to ERN 7107, please, that page number. Okay. If you look from the sixth line from the bottom of the page on the right, you see what's attributed to Mr. Beara beginning with the words "Nemam buraz." You see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I don't have it, broth. Let's just -- the only way is through the administration." But just a moment, I think that in the audio, you can hear "burazer." Please, can you tell me the date of this recording? Can you give me the time and the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can certainly give you the date, which I think I've indicated as 5th December 1995. The time, I don't have for you at the moment, but I will get it for you if you need it. In the interim let me turn to -- first let me confirm with you that the word --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the audio recording says "burazer." That's a mistake in the printed version, and there's an abundance of errors in the printed versions, and the word in this one is "burazer."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is that substantively distinctive from a linguistic perspective from the other times you've seen the word in the other intercepts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? "Buraz" and "burazer"? Is that what you are referring to? If you allow me to say that "sjor" and "burazer" do not have identical meanings. Sjor is indeed a marked Cakavian version. One can only encounter it in the coastal area, and it's a Romanic word, whereas "burazer" is of the Turkish origin and is used throughout the entire Serbian linguistic area. Five days ago I had a call from my brother, and he asked me, and I quote, "burazer, or broth, when are you coming back?" The secretary of the Serbian Academy of Science and Arts, Radisav Boskovic, in the ten years that he spent in this post addressed me hundreds of times with the words such as "burazer," among others. It has been used if one wants to emphasize something and most commonly if one wants to put forward a different opinion, such as, this is not like that, broth, or my broth, you can hear it in the films, in the TV series produced by the Belgrade television. Anyway, the word "burazer" can be checked in the Serbian dictionaries. The shortened version, "buraz," is more common in the west, notably in Bosnia, more so than in Serbia. Therefore, "burazer" is not a marked word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Remetic, I put these questions to you because in your report, you wrote that you considered the absence of the words "sjor," "gospon," and "burazer" in the intercepts that you examined. Now you're telling me, apparently, that the word "burazer" has absolutely no linguistic significance. So my question to you is, Why is that something that you paid attention to in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. I think it mischaracterizes his report, and I think the professor as he's tried to explain it, but it certainly mischaracterizes it as the question has been put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can read what's in the report into the record if that will help my colleague a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, and Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely, I wanted to have the reference for this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think I referred to it initially when I began the examination, but I'll refer to it again. It's at page 17 of the report. It's in the second paragraph of the English version of the report, and it reads as follows: "The noun "sjor," represents a typical borrowing from the romance languages that has taken root mainly in coastal areas and suggest someone who has lived on the sea coast for awhile. However, in the corpus of 18 transcripts, it occurs only once. This is quite symptomatic considering that words such as "sjor," "gospon," "burazer," and the like occur frequently in the every day speech of people who use them, while this is lacking in the transcripts I examined." I put it to you, sir, that the transcripts that you examined actually do contain the word "burazer" as you have written it in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, honestly, but I think he is mischaracterizing and misunderstand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can he mischaracterize -- how can he mischaracterise if he's been reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, because -- look at his question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, Mr. -- stop. Please answer the question, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this refers only to the word "sjor," which is supposed to be heard quite often because it's a custom that this type of word such as "sjor," "gospon," and "burazer" means that "burazer" is being used unlike "sjor," and that's why I said it wasn't enough. It is said previously that the Turkish originated word "burazer" or its abbreviated version "buraz" is not territorially restricted or limited, although it occurs more often in the western area, therefore including Bosnia. More precisely in everyday life on TV, on the radio, and in direct communications, the word "burazer" can also be heard in Serbia as well. "Sjor" and "burazer" do not have the same meaning in our profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you taking issue, sir, with the fact that Mr. Beara uses the term "burazer" rather frequently? Are you taking some contrary position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that he used to use it, just as I'm not denying that I or my relatives or my friends are using it. My brother whenever he calls me, he says "bro" or "broth," but sir, the word "sjor" does not appear, and that's an indicative word that can serve as a repetitive indicator, but it doesn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you consider the use of the word "burazer" in the intercepts that you examined in the context of determining whether or not the speaker was Mr. Beara, or did you disregard it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I took everything into consideration; however, everything was not -- was very little. It was a limited corpus. I said that several times. It was limited in terms of quantity. From the linguistic point of view, it's so one-sided and thin. We see short orders, short questions, short answers without any context. I look at it as a whole. I found the word "buraz" more appropriate for the western area. In Bosnia and Serbia, you will more often find the word "burazer," and I took it as one of the elements, and I weighed the facts that either speak against or for it; that is, for the assumption that we are talking about Mr. Beara. I wrote in my report that I performed my job by looking for the elements, the proof, the foundation for establishing the link between the transcript and Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, but my question was a yes-or-no question. Did you consider that term or the frequency of that term in terms of determining whether or not Mr. Beara was the speaker on the intercept?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised it as a fact, but I repeat again that the most important thing for me was the situation referring to the long "jat," where you can clearly discern variants.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you gave it a different degree of weight in terms of identifying the speaker. That's fair to say, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by giving it -- in my view whether he said "podijeliti" or "podjelit" has more weight than whether he used the word "burazer" because "burazer" is not marked in terms of variants and territory, whereas the other one is. If the word "sjor" occurred as many times as did the word "burazer," then it would have had a proper weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, you're a linguist. Are you familiar with the term --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're familiar with the term an idiodialect, right? Are you familiar with that term, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if you would, tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An idiodialect is, let's say, a personal linguistic expression of an individual that is being formed over a period of time. It is recognisable and it identifies this particular person. It's a linguistic system used by an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. It can also incorporate patterns of speech, can't it, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm an English-speaking person, and I use the word "man" quite frequently in my speech. That is a pattern of my speech that is identifiable. Did you, sir, consider Mr. Beara's pattern of speech independently of his dialect in terms of determining who was speaking on the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the company of Mr. Beara for seven or eight hours listening to him speaking. I myself took part in the conversations, and all I can say is that I found it very impressive that he was so calm and composed. I noticed that he is using the colloquial Split dialect that the input of a standard language came from the Croatian standard language; however, there was not enough time for me to notice these phrases, these patterns, as you say, "hey, man," "listen, man," as you say is used in English, or "burazer." I did not observe any frequency of usage because there was not enough time. There was not enough possibility. Had we had an opportunity to talk alone in a relaxed manner, I may have found it out, but it was sufficient for me to see that I had in front of me a person who speaks Cakavian dialect and the person who comes from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, the reason I ask you this, I just want to make sure we are talking about the same thing. When you say that you didn't have a chance to observe this, you are talking about during the course of your 7- or 8-hour interview with Mr. Beara back in April. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is whether or not you made any observations with respect to that as concerns the intercepts that are attributed to Mr. Beara. In other words, is there a commonality in the idiodialect found in the intercepts that are attributed to Mr. Beara separately and apart from a dialectological analysis of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the analysis, and the OTP themselves arrived at that conclusion, if I'm not mistaken, a certain percentage of these transcripts have not been linked to Beara. Furthermore, some of them are so brief and fragmented that they do not constitute a corpus, and it is inappropriate to make any serious linguistic judgement on them. And also, what has been said is that these transcripts do not correspond to one another in linguistic terms. It has been said quite clearly and precisely that in places there is an incongruous between the transcripts and the typed versions. I would like to remind you that on the 1st of August, the talks or the conversations held in the morning and in the afternoon is something that -- which I described as a mixture. A person without a conscientious effort cannot do that. I as a dialectologist can say the same thing in different dialects, but I'm nearly at the end of my career. Secondly, about the report and the 15th of July, I mentioned the dilemma, whether there was one transcript or three transcripts. This is what I described as "leopard skin". What can one discern as a specificity in a leopard skin if there are such huge differences? In a nutshell, the transcripts do not contain enough consistent and uniformed text in order to demonstrate a possible specific feature of the speaker or possible specific traits. I would like to remind you that all the words that are linked to Mr. Beara according to the operative workers, when I type them into the computer, what came up was 2 and a half pages of text; nearly half of it can be discarded as minor details, meaningless words, and in the remaining part you have different things. You don't have consistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. Remetic. What I'd like to know and what I think I was trying to get at was, as you see, as I pointed out to you, the word "burazer," or "buraz" shows up in a number of intercepts apparently attributable to Mr. Beara. It shows up in 65 ter 3607. That's the one of December 5th, 1995. It shows up on one, two, three occasions in that intercept. It shows up on the one dated 6/6/1995 on one occasion. It shows up in an intercept - bear with me one moment, please - dated 13th August, 1995, one, two -- two occasions. It shows up in another intercept. I'm sorry. That was 65 ter 3627 for the record. It shows up in 65 ter 3626, as well, on one, two, three, four occasions. And it shows up in the intercept dated 15 July 1995, as I went through with you, on one occasion. It shows up on the intercept dated 13 July 1995 on two separate occasions as I've showed you, and the 65 ter number for that intercept is 1130. In addition to that, I wondered if you noticed or paid attention to whether or not Mr. Beara was prone to use, I don't know, foreign words in his language, in his particular means of speaking. And what I'd like to do is draw your attention, if I could, to the August 1st, 1995, intercept, which is 65 ter 1380. Yes, that intercept is at 2245 hours. There are a couple of words I'd just like to draw your attention to on that intercept. If I could have the -- okay. Great. Now, if I could just go to the second page of the B/C/S. All right. It's the last paragraph of that intercept. It ends with the words -- it looks like "ceka dalje." Do you see that? It's on the right-hand side of the screen in front of you. It's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in that sentence, that is the line immediately above that --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I can't see it. Where is that? "Ceka dalje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [French spoken] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we get to do French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [French spoken] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I don't know if I'm the only one receiving the interpretation in French. Okay. All right. So there is something to be rectified. You can continue, Professor, in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just, if I could, orient you to where -- what I'm talking about. Do you see the words "burazer," and there's a number 999 in the middle of the page on the right? All right. It's the paragraph immediately preceding that starts with looks like --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Do you see that? If we could just --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see -- "ijerko ova [phoen]." I can't see that. "Hello, I'm here." "Hello, I'm here."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It's above that. It's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I've just called the boss" -- oh right. Yes, I can see that. Oh, this person from Uzice says, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in that paragraph, you see the word -- the words -- it says "drugi" and then is says "befel [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drugi befel? Yes. Close and wait, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what the word "befel" means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order. An order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's of German origin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Befel, befel. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How about the word "muchachos?" Are you familiar with that term?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Los muchachos. I'm not familiar with the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. How about the word --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. You asked me about the word "burazer," did you not? If I may, you have put quite a number of questions. Let's deal with the word "burazer" first, if I may. "Burazer" -- based on the word "burazer," which appears quite often, I could not link any of the transcripts to Ljubisa Beara because every Ljubo in the army could use the word "burazer" just like my brother does because it's widely used across the country, and that's where the problem arises from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. What I'm asking you about in particular is whether you considered whether or not Mr. Beara had a tendency to use foreign words, words that are outside his normal dialect or influence from foreign origins in his speech, in his speech, he particularly as opposed to he from the Cakavian, Ekavian group of people, speaking people. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice that he would do that more commonly than other people that I normally communicate with, and if you allow me, I can illustrate this by saying that you will hear in the conversations, this is how it is and "schluss." Even people who don't speak German will use this German word, "schluss" or "schloss," and "schluss" in this case is just a confirmation that people will use foreign words. Languages have no boundaries. We are all exposed to foreign influences from radio, TV, and all of our expressions are full of foreign words. I have not noticed Ljubisa Beara being any different from either me or anybody else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not phrasing this as clearly as I would hope. When you examined the text of the intercepts you analysed, did you consider the fact that that text contained language attributed to Mr. Beara which had in it foreign words in order to determine whether or not it was likely -- it likely originated from Mr. Beara? That's all I'm asking, is whether you considered, and if you didn't, then the answer is no; and if you did, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at dialects, and "sjor" appeared once and never again. As for the word "burazer," I've already said that it is not marked. As for the rest, I did not pay particular attention to foreign expressions or words that are not so common in the transcripts. They are rather few and far between, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's those rather few and far between transcripts that are at all attributable to Mr. Beara; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my view, only one with -- a huge, big reservation, in my view. If anybody has firm arguments to prove that they indeed may be attributed to Beara, I would be curious to see those. The 1st of August, the conversation in the morning, is most congruent with what Ljubisa Beara is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, then my question is, when you saw the word befel in the 1st August, 1995, intercept at 2245, 65 ter 1380, did you consider it in light of having later seen 65 ter 3626 in which the term "Los Muchachos" is used allegedly attributed to Mr. Beara? Did you consider -- and did you consider that in terms of 65 ter 3627 where the term "professional" is attributed to Mr. Beara, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there's a Serbian proverb which says, One swallow does not spring make. Just one example extracted from a whole is too little to lead to any major conclusions, and as for befel, you will hear that in conversations with people who will say, what's up, did the little wife send you a befel, meaning that did your wife order you to do something, implying that women give orders to their husband. I would say this word is not marked; it's not indicative; it's not enough to seriously identify a person. Judgements on -- made at least in my profession based on facts. The more facts there are, the more reliable the judgement is; and another thing, the problem are counter-arguments, those that eliminate rather than confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and I thank you for your answer, but it is interesting that you reference this proverb, which is one swallow does not spring make, and that's one example extracted from a whole is too little to lead to any major conclusions because what you did in this case --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one swallow. That's what I said. One swallow, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you in this case in your report is you analysed no more than nine intercepts that alleged that Mr. Beara is speaking over a period of about a month. That's what covers the intercept range of the ones you examined, and you concluded based upon what amounts to no more than 2 and a half pages, half of which you said you could discard, that you could exclude Mr. Beara as the speaker in several intercepts, this based upon a 7- or 9-hour initial interview with Mr. Beara, but I'll get to the specifics of that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at all the transcripts, and in some there are no linguistic facts at all. I did not force any exclusive judgements. My judgements would say that there's nothing to link the transcript to Mr. Beara, especially in the context of his -- today's utterance, the way he speaks today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to, if I could, go to the appendix of your report. 2D551. I think we have it there on the right. It might be useful to have the English version in here as well. Okay. All right. Now, the first thing I wanted to point out was the code that you used, and you can see on the right-hand side of your screen. I think it may be on the second page of the English, but in any event, you did describe that somewhat on direct, so I don't want to belabour the issue. Zero indicates that there's insufficient data, and I take it that you mean that there's insufficient data to draw any conclusion with respect to the categories that you've indicated above, which is -- which are, Participant revealed himself or was revealed as Beara; does the dialect clearly reveal the speaker's origin; is the dialect strongly tied to a certain area; and lastly, is the speaker's dialect close to Ljubisa Beara's current manner of speech? When you say zero with respect to those categories, it means you don't have sufficient information to draw a conclusion one way or another, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you indicate with a negative, well, it's obvious. You mean that those criteria are not fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And a positive the contrary, that the category is fulfilled, has been met, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So where you've indicated zero, that does not exclude Mr. Beara as a potential participant in the conversation that you are examining, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are usually conversations where there's no text, no words at all, where he is in one way or another indirectly implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question has to do with whether or not your analysis -- well, whether or not the indication of zero is an exclusive or inclusive designation or a neutral designation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This certainly does not include Mr. Beara because there's no data. There are no elements that would include him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So among the intercepts that you examined, intercept at -- on July 13th, 1919 - that's at 65 ter 1147 - that particular intercept doesn't mention Beara at all; and therefore, you indicate that it has apparently no linguistic value, or you are unable to ascertain any linguistic value from that intercept. That's a better statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to intercept 13 July, 1945, that is 65 ter 1148, same conclusion, you can't extrapolate from that intercept any useful information with respect to Mr. Beara; and in fact, there's a reference to Mr. Beara in that intercept but not as the speaker, right? There's a reference to Ljubisa, I should say, to be accurate, but not as the speaker, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is mentioned, but I believe that the OTP says Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin here. So if I'm not mistaken, according to the OTP this is a different Ljubisa rather than Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I accept that, Mr. Remetic, but I would assume that you when you conducted your analysis of these intercepts, you used your independent judgment to determine what was what and not what the OTP represented or what the Defence counsel represented, I assume?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may object to the form of the question, and it's mischaracterisation. I think the professor in his report clearly indicates that he utilized the Prosecution's understanding or interpretation of some of these intercepts, but nowhere does -- or nowhere did we give our interpretation of these intercepts at any time to the professor, so it certainly mischaracterises it. But in his report he isolates which exactly work he performed, and that included looking at what the Prosecution's position was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mea, he's just querying for a confirmation, asking a confirmation from the witness that he used an independent judgement. That's how I understand it. I mean -- Judge Kwon? Yeah. Let's move. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to July 13th or 13 July intercept at 2305 at 65 ter 1153, for the record: Now, in that case there's a reference to Ljubo but, he cannot be heard, and that provided you with no useful linguistic information, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a linguist, yes, there was no work for me there. This allegedly is a monologue by General Mladic, which was out of my scope of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. With respect to the 15th July intercept at 0952, this is 65 ter 1177 for the record, and that is an entry indicating that Beara is looking for General Zivanovic, and you derive no linguistic value from that intercept either, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operator says what he says, and I analyse what is denoted by B, Beara, colonel or whatever the code name may be, and there's none of that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. 16 July at 2233 hours. That one you've indicated all zeros for all four categories. It's 65 ter 1204, and similarly you derive no linguistic value from that intercept?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. 23rd July at 805 - July '95 for the record - 805, and 65 ter 1310. There's a mention of a Ljubo in there but not as a speaker. So that was of no linguistic value to you as well, right? I'm sorry. You have to answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, yes, yes. It's empty. There's nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 2nd August, 13 00 hours. That is 65 ter 1395. That is also an intercept that mentions Beara but not as the speaker.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was no linguistic value to you, and you issued -- and you indicated that by placing zeros in all four relevant categories, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's 16 July at 1111 hours. That's 65 ter 1187, and you've indicated that although there is an indication that Mr. Beara identifies himself as Beara, there's otherwise insufficient linguistic information for your analysis, so you put a plus where it says "participant revealed himself or was revealed as Beara" and zeros for the remaining three categories, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 July, 1111, yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And on the 25th of July, 1995, 0709. That's 65 ter 1328 [Realtime transcript read in error, "1028] for the record. You have indicated a negative for "participant revealed himself or was revealed as Beara," and you've indicated zeros for the remaining categories. In fact, in that intercept somebody is identified as Ljubo, but that was of no linguistic value to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. No. Very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So what we're talking about here in terms of the relevant intercepts for your analysis or the intercepts you say you were able to analyse are 13 July at 1009; 15 July at 0954, 0955, 0957, 10 a.m.; on 1 August at 2245, 2308; and on 2nd August, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, I think also the 1st of August at 1002, which we covered, but it doesn't seem to have made it in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. 1002 is the one intercept in which you say you were able to positively link to Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's mischaracterization, but we'll let the record stand as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So we're talking about eight intercepts where you say there's not sufficient information to attribute -- well, let me rephrase that. This negative answer that you gave, so those intercepts cannot be attributed to Mr. Beara as per your analysis. Eight, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attributed one with a reservation. I allow for this for a possibility. As for the others, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just for the record, previous page, page 52, line 25: Is that number correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just trying to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number of the intercept of 25th of July, 0709.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, it should be 1328. I'm sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You've indicated that - I believe you indicated, and you correct me if I'm wrong - you didn't review any testimony of the intercept operators that were involved in these particular intercepts that you analysed; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read the operator's statements. I said yesterday that some of them come from my municipality from the region where I come from. I read them very carefully, and I realized what difficulties they had in their work. And I said yesterday that in a certain manner, these operators and I are colleagues. I recorded at least 1.000 hours of conversations and listened to at least 2.000 hours of conversations of the recorded material. I also read Nijo's [phoen] critic and his opinion on how these operators worked and under what conditions they worked, and we agreed to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. What I'm trying to do is I just want to clarify for the record what it is that you looked at and what it is that you didn't look at. So I want to distinguish for you between statements and the testimony, and my question is to you, is did you review the testimony in addition to the statements, or did you review only the statements of these operators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I had their statements in my hand in which they say that they were aware of the possibility of being called to testify before the Court. One of them was asked if he remembered the conversation and the transcript, and I think that one that is linked to Mr. Beara and Konjevic Polje, and he said that the handwriting resembled his but that another operator – (redacted) (redacted). He couldn't exactly recall who took part in the conversation. The only thing he could remember was that they had problems with a tank at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you for one second, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session one second, please? If we could go into private session for one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just so that -- rather than belabour this issue, just -- the documents that you were provided that you looked at are listed in your report. That's fair, right? That's in section 5 of the material. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that you are aware, it doesn't actually list any testimony in here, so just so you know that. Now, you said earlier, I think that was yesterday --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it's a mistake, then. No, sir, so this means these are their statements. Okay, they are statements, not testimonies, so we have here a terminological error, and I do beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No problem with that, Mr. Remetic. No problem at all. You mentioned yesterday, and that was yesterday's transcript at page 11, lines 15 through 20, I don't know if it's been updated and changed, but you said that "The degree of reliability in determining the identity is directly proportional to the quantity of linguistic facts and the core of facts available to the expert who wishes to determine the identity in question. The more, the wealthier the core of linguistic facts, the higher the chances of success." And then it says, "Viscosity of linguistic fact ..." and it appears that there was something in the transcript that didn't make it, that wasn't transcribed, "... makes the call more difficult." As you said, the corpus of the material that you considered for analysis amounted to no more than 2 and a half pages; that's true, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that half of that material was completely useless and could be discarded, I think is the term you used; that's right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That leaves us with about a page and a quarter of useful information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. I didn't measure it precisely with a calculator. What is relevant is relative, but in absolute terms it's a very poor material. Never in my life had I had to work with a poorer material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, then, it's fair to say that the poorer the material, the less reliable the conclusions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are difficult to reach, the conclusions, I mean. Scientists are reluctant to make conclusions based on few facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, scientists are also reluctant to make conclusions based upon facts that they cannot quantify and measure; that's true too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caution is a good ally. Caution is a good partner in one's job. Of course they are reluctant. We are talking about percentages, about the degree of probability. We are talking about nuances. You know, science is not a dogma; linguistics cannot be classified as a yes or no science. You can't measure it in kilograms. You have to assess the probabilities and the possibilities, and one tends to choose the one which seems to him to be the most credible and the most sustainable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm glad that you mentioned the word "science" because I wanted to ask you about that too. When you make a determination as you did in this case that a given intercept is incompatible with the manner of speech of Mr. Beara in April of this year, when you make that kind of a determination, what is the probability of error with respect to that conclusion? How is that measured in linguistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one were to make a judgement on how the language of the transcripts and the expressions linked to the name of Mr. Beara stand within the context of the present speech or the one heard on the 7th or the 8th of April, my profession would demand that all these transcripts be rejected a priori, in advance. I said yesterday what approach I took to this task. I'm not sure whether it's a good and proper approach. I was seeking a possibility for establishing a definite link to Mr. Beara - I also said yesterday and I reiterate it again today - in free communications in a more informal and relaxed conversation in a colloquial Split-based Cakavian dialect. Whenever there are any inputs of standard language, that's the Zagreb-based standard Croatian, and I allowed for this possibility in the transcript as well. A person using a dialect, and especially a high-ranking officer, most commonly will use standard language, and this is what has been said, that this transcripts were made in a relatively good standard language, and I suppose that Beara spoke in the Zagreb-Croatian language. In the 1st of August transcript is the place where I found the most elements to establish this link. I never said that this is the only thing and absolute thing. This is not a dogma. There are no absolute truths or very few absolute truths, but I say that I found it more plausible that the factors that it's his outweighed the others. So when Beara is using the dialect and the standard language, I took this option into the consideration, as well; and therefore, I allowed for the possibility that it was him speaking there. Unfortunately, there is no transcript written by the hand of the operator concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well -- all right. Thank you for that. What it sounds to me like you are saying is that you did the best you could under the circumstances you were presented with. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, sir, and I spent a lot of time doing this job. It was a difficult one, an unusual one, and I did my best on the basis of the available facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also sounds to me like you have some reservations as to whether or not the approach you took was good and proper within the scientific domain of linguistics, which is why you say that if it were considered that -- in those terms, these transcripts wouldn't even be considered, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see -- excuse me, I'm not quite sure I understand your question completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask it is different way. When you said I'm not sure that this approach is good, did you mean that you are not sure that the techniques that you used because you had to in these circumstances are acceptable for a linguist from a scientific point of view? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant something else. I almost took the same position as you did towards this material. I was looking for something on the basis of which I can link the transcript to Mr. Beara, so I analyse every single word, whether "sjor" was enough. It wasn't enough. It wasn't mentioned enough. Is "burazer" enough? No, it was not because it was being used throughout the whole area. The infinitive was not also sufficient because it was counterposed by some other form. You see that every little detail was analysed, and then on the whole if arguments A and B -- and I repeat, that was a poor corpus of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think this is a good time to break with the Court's permission if I'm right about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have? Do you think you will finish with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not pushing you. I mean, I'm just querying to see whether we should keep the next witness here or not. I mean, that's the reason why I put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a fair question. I think I'll be an hour with him yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have an hour. We have three-quarters of an hour when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think I've answered your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it you have a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, 15 to 20 minutes, but if we can release the witness, maybe, because I think -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, this is why I put the question, I mean, not to push either of you. Madam Registrar, if you could kindly arrange with the Victims and Witnesses -- okay. Thank you. And explain to her, explain to her what happened. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. I want to apologise for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go, go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Remetic. Okay. Last off -- last we left off - I'm sorry - I was asking you about the science aspect of the analysis that you performed in relation to these intercepts. Now, one thing I do want to ask you is, in your analysis of these intercepts, with respect to the possibility of identifying Mr. Beara, did you look specifically at elements of language for the purpose of including Mr. Beara as a possible source of the text, conversation, or did you look at elements of language for the purpose of excluding Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said before the break, or I was about to say, that basically I was seeking such features that could potentially identify Mr. Beara; that means linguistic facts that carry weight of a reliable proof that there was sufficient quantity of these facts and that they are of a differential type. In other words, that they can be linked to a specific area, a specific variant, and a specific dialect region. Only in the alleged conversation of the 1st August for which we do not have a manuscript, regrettably, I would have preferred to have one, I allowed for a higher degree of possibility that it was uttered by Mr. Beara. I say Beara in the context of the standard language of the region in which he served for 20 years and which he adopted as his own dialect. He adopted the Split dialect as his own, but when he uses the standard language, as I said many times before, it was the common variant of the Croatian language, which is nowadays the standard Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think in your direct testimony you refer to the specific discipline of linguistics that you are involved in as dialectological linguistics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you are aware, of course, that there are other fields of linguistics or subdisciplines of linguistics that are applicable to a forensic analysis such as the one that you've undertaken with respect to these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not possible to make a proper phonetic analysis. A proper phonetic analysis requires a high quality audio recording or a professional dialectologist noting down somebody's speech in his notebook. The best Serbian study on the Serbian dialectology was published in 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was the time when audio recordings were not available but good professionals and scholars took notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So a phonetic linguistic analysis is not possible based upon the material that you had at your disposal, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An accurate one. You don't have the timbre of the voice; you don't have the timbre of the consonants; you don't have the accents; you don't have the prosodia; and these are all the basis on one immediately recognised the origin of a person who is talking. The accent is revealing; it cannot be concealed, especially some of its traits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you've indicated in your report that you yourself would able to identify Mr. Beara's voice if you heard it on a tape; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to a phonetic linguistic analysis, you could also regard this material from the point of view of a sociolinguistic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent. Sociolinguistics can provide that, and that was taken into consideration. The influence of the environments, the influence of the professional environment is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That also has to do with the acquisition of a particular dialect, right, the circumstances under which a person might use a secondary dialect if they have one, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All of the influences that go into determining whether or not a person speaks with one dialect as opposed to another; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's a phenomenon known in co -- known in sociolinguistics is code-shifting, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you took that information into consideration, of course, when you met with Mr. Beara back in April of this year and when you reviewed the corpus of the intercept text, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The present way in which Mr. Beara speaks and his code-shifting, basically, from one model of speech to another can only be explained within the context of social linguistics. The Split dialect is a prestigious one. The people of Split foster their speech, and they are proud of it. They do not try to avoid it or suppress it. The Split community has a high rating both before and now, and anyone who wishes to integrate him or herself into this community must accept and adopt its way of communications, its communication codes, which Mr. Beara did. In my view, he knowingly adopted the Split dialect as his own, and this attitude he did not change even after the war and all the consequences left in the wake of the war. I think that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that answer. Your analysis of this material was based upon primarily dialectological analysis, right, a dialectological evaluation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the analysis was based on everything. I looked at the context of the person's dialect and also the variance of the Serbian or Croatian standard language. If I had adhered strictly to dialect only, I would have rejected everything as irrelevant for the analysis after my conversation with Mr. Beara in the month of April of this year. I put everything in the context of the Serbo-Croatian standard language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, but what I mean is in your report you don't mention anything about the phenomenon known as code-shifting, which we've just discussed, which determines whether or not a person who is bidialectical uses one dialect versus another dialect in any given circumstance. There's nothing in your report concerning that sociolinguistic phenomena. So my question to you is, did you consider that and if so, why isn't it in your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there has been a misunderstanding. I said and I'm sure you will find it in my report that it is difficult to devise and decipher how it could have happened that a person who was born in Sarajevo as an Ikavian and Cakavian has turned into a Cakavian and Ikavian speaker. You will find it in my report, sir. I'm sure of that. How could that person have forgotten that Cakavian dialect during the war or at least for the 15 days when the intercepts were taken, and how was it possible for that same person to return to that Cakavian dialect after the war? There is no doubt in my mind that that's how he spoke before the war or even more consistently. I mentioned that in my report, and I also say in my report that we have before us a phenomenon of somebody who drowns his linguistic identity into something else, into something foreign. People who surrounded him even said that they didn't know that he was not a Croat until the war began, and then when he joined the Army of Republika Srpska they thought there that he was a Croat, which means that his dialect was such as it was, and it still remains to be the same to this day, and it is in sharp collusion with what I can read in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, you posed the question, and the question is how can somebody's dialect change from one period of time to another period of time and revert at yet another period of time? And the answer to that question as you well know is found in the literature of social linguistics and is particularly well known that it is found within the particular phenomenon in social linguistics as code-shifting. You know that, and so my question to you is, why doesn't that appear in your report as opposed to the question that you posed? Why isn't the answer there, if you considered it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I looked at the transcripts. Within this context, a Cakavian and an Ikavian before the war, a Cakavian and an Ikavian after the war, what we are talking about probably does not belong to that Cakavian person. That would be the healthiest logic that I can come up with. This is something that I cannot explain. If any of these transcripts may be attributed to Ljubisa Beara, how did this all happen? And there is something else. There are situations that differ from one another in communication. There are also functional styles. There are different registers. For example, there is allegedly chat among friends on the one hand, and on the other hand there is public speaking. Standard language is more commonly used in official situations, at conferences when you are standing at a rostrum, when you write a text or a report or a review. It is within that context that I looked for possibilities to link Beara or the person denoted as Beara with the western variant of the standard language which prevails in these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that answer. You've indicated -- well, let me ask you this. With respect to whether or not a person has a command of varying dialects or various dialects, in this particular instance you've put in your report that Mr. Beara has an infallible command of Ekavian, Ikavian and Ijekavian. That's in your report at page 14, right? I'll read it to you. It's in the middle of the page in the English in 14, and it starts --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've got it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's what your report says, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's relevant to the determining whether or not he has the ability and the skill to change his dialect, right, if he has an infallible command of them? It's relevant; you can answer that one yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not saying that he is in full command. I'm just saying that he is aware of all the distinctions. He did not use Ekavian first and then Ikavian and then Ijekavian to enable me to say that he is in full command. I asked him concretely about some forms that I found in the transcripts, and he answered matter-of-factly, no, I'm not a Serbian, this is not me. He knows how Serbians speak, he also knows how Montenegrins speak, and he knows how people speak in different areas. He is aware of all the distinctions. However, when you write that somebody is in full command, that person should be able to demonstrate all that. He demonstrated well the Cakavian, Ikavian dialect of the Split area within the seven hours that I spent with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, with all due respect what is written in your report and perhaps is a translation error or a translation misconception is that "Even" -- you wrote, "Even today after sometime spent in Belgrade, he manifests a certain distancing from Ikavian. We reiterate" - in bold - "that he has an infallible command of the Ekavian, Ikavian, and Ijekavian distinctions, which was confirmed to us by listening to his conversations with other individuals present..." et cetera, et cetera. The word of "command" is not one that originates from me. That's what's in your report, and you can see that. Is that right, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I'm not able to find where this is. I would like to be able to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, the closest I can find in the text is a bold section, a bold part of the text in section 7 of your report, and it immediately follows that section where it says Ikavian, Ekavian, Ijekavian, Bosnian, Montenegrin, Serbian, in bold in your report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, yes. Now I've got it. Yes, I've got it now. Thank you. It says here, he, and we repeat, has an infallible command of the Ekavian, Ikavian, and Ijekavian distinctions, and we were able to convince ourselves of that while listening to their conversation with other interlocutors followed by a cross-examination, and so on and so forth. Maybe this has been put in too simple terms terminologically. He knows how things are said by other persons. When he says lipodite [phoen], he knows where people say lipodeta [phoen] and where they say lijepodijeta [phoen]. He knows where people say ditza [phoen], where they say djetza [phoen], and where they say dijetza [phoen]. He is aware of that. He is aware of the distinctions, but he is not using those words. He had never demonstrated usage. He is only aware of those things. He even has a negative attitude towards Ekavian and none of that towards Ijekavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether or not he used it. I asked you whether or not he had a command of it, and that's what your report says, isn't it -- doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knows how people speak in different areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's relevant to an assessment as to whether or not he has the capacity to use it, whether or not he has the ability to use a different dialect other than the one you observed. It's relevant, is my point. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he can distinguish between different dialects, but he certainly can distinguish between the variances of the standard language. There are a lot of dialects which are different. I myself am not able to use all sorts of dialects in my speech. Please, bear that in mind because there is a difference there. He probably may be able to use Ekavian, but I'm not sure whether he would be able to use Ijekavian correctly, but with speaking about the variances of the standard language whereas there are a lot of dialects in all the variances of the standard language, in all three of them, the Ekavian, the Ijekavian, and the Ikavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Remetic. Thank you for that. You also indicate in your report, also on page 14, that Mr. Beara as you observed is of high intelligence, that he has an obviously enviable general cultural background, and that he is well read, right? And these are all sociological phenomena that contribute to an evaluation of his abilities as concerns by dialectism, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is an intelligent man, and any intelligent man finds it easy to cope with all sorts of situations, and he certainly is an intelligent person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the reliability -- well, before I get to that, in terms of your analysis here, you said that the reliability of your conclusions are directly related to the amount of linguistic relevant material that you have before you. That's true, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in an analysis of this type, can you point to any literature, document, or protocol that tells you how much meaningful linguistic information you have to have in any given document in order to make the attribution of identity as you have done in this case? How many words have to appear? How far apart do they have to be? How many times do they have to appear in order for you to make the kind of connection or disassociation that you make in relation to these particular intercepts? Is there any methodological material you can point us to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no rule. There are no percentages or set numbers, but in principle it is clear: The higher the quantity of the facts, the higher the degree of reliability of any evaluation. Not all the facts are equally relevant. There are differences based on which speeches may be classified. We said it already that in our language one thing is jat and the other is accent. The accent is completely missing here, and there's very little jat to be found in these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Among the intercepts that you have indicated negative values for the four categories you've provided in your annex, among those intercepts, how is a Court going to determine among those intercepts what degree of reliability is claimed as to each one of those intercepts? How is the Court going to determine that when you indicate negative for Intercept X and you indicate negative for Intercept Y that you are talking about the same degree of reliability or a close degree of reliability as to either one? How does that occur without the ability to quantify your results?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that some conversations where I had only five, six, or seven words which were completely meaningless or of no relevance for the topic that was being discussed did not allow for any possibility of linkage. In other transcripts where there were more facts provided, I looked at those that might provide a differentiation, that might be marked as being linked to western areas or to the western variance of the standard language, and to the dialect or the conversational patterns of the area where Beara had lived. I did not find that. I did not find identifying facts that might have linked him to those alleged intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you've indicated that there's no rule, which means that you cannot make a quantitative assessment as to the level of reliability that's indicated in your report. That's correct, right, other than to say it's likely or unlikely or consistent or inconsistent, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact, it's not possible for you to quantify in terms of the linguistic significance each of the words that contribute to the finding that you've made as to whether or not it likely -- whether or not the intercept likely encompasses Mr. Beara or excludes Mr. Beara. That's true too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in the absence of standards of quantification in terms of the reliability of the results and in terms of the reliability of the information contributing to the results, it makes what you've done in this case impossible for another person to repeat or replicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another person?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Another linguist examining the same material as you might very well reach a completely different conclusion in terms of the ability to attribute certain intercepts or include Mr. Beara as a potential participant in an intercept or excluding him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To compare others with oneself is beside the point, and if somebody were to arrive at a different conclusion, I would like to see their arguments for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fair enough, but what I'm talking about in particular, as you are well aware, is the scientific method, and the scientific method necessarily incorporates the concept of verification, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Verification entails a standardized means by which results can be checked, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you are telling me there's no rule; ergo, there's no standardized means by which your results can be checked, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, there's no standard. The basic features of properties of dialect are well known. Furthermore, the relevant features are also known, and they can be used to speak about the variances of what until recently was our common language. Those are very well known, and based on those I carried out my analysis. I had all those in mind when I embarked on my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, what you are doing here in terms of your forensic analysis of these intercepts is effectively you are making an identification; that's true, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything boils down to identification, and everything boils down to the question whether these intercepts may be linked to the name of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The identification that you are making is based upon something indemning to a person that is inherently mutable, right? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's something I could not check because there was nothing to base my verification on. The only thing I had were transcripts, and that's what I used in my work. One could check only if one had the audio recordings of all the transcripts that I analysed. Second of all -- I don't see anything else, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me point something out to you. A dialect is something that can change. You can -- we can agree on that, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything changes. Dialects are no exception. Civilisation makes its mark. What do you mean when you say that? Do you mean that a person changes his or her dialect, or do you mean that a dialect changes with evolution, a dialect as a system -- as something that undergoes changes, or are you referring to me as a person who is able to change his dialect and go through different dialects at different times? What do you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's a perfectly fair question. I apologise if my question was too broad. What I'm talking to you about is in the context of individual identification. So when I say a dialect can change, I'm talking about on an individual level, through exposure to other people, through moving from one place to another, through taking up jobs in certain locations and moving back home. All of those contribute to the change and development of a person's dialect --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- individually, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Dialect can change more easily than, for example, somebody's height as an adult, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one has to take into consideration a number of factors when we speak about changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several factors. Firstly, the age. A young person, a child will be more susceptible to changing his or her dialect if they change environments. That's one thing. Secondly, the prestigiousness of a dialect, whether you have arrived into a community which is reputable or prestigious or -- in other words, whether this change is beneficial to you. You are entering a new environment which is more developed in terms of culture or industrial achievement, et cetera, and it requires you to adapt to it. Furthermore, it depends on the professional profile of the person in question. A less literate person, a less educated person will more quickly shift and give up his own dialect, so as I say, there are a number of factors. There are people who are economically inferior, and they always adapt to those who are economically superior, and they will more readily accept someone who is superior to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Remember, I'm not talking at a social level. I'm talking about an individual level, that somebody's DNA, eye colour, and height are less mutable than their dialect as a general principle. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So for the purposes of a forensic identification process, what you are studying is something that is inherently more malleable, changeable than other forensic identification sciences, right, such as DNA identification, fingerprint-processing, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And all those forensic activities can establish a known rate of error with respect to the processes that they employ, that is, the chance of a random error given the processes that you undertake. My question, therefore, to you is, given what you've said today, can you tell us, what is the random rate of error, the known or predictable rate of error with respect to the analysis that you performed on these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those who do nothing do not make mistakes, and I don't see where the errors are, and I cannot see that I could have done any better job than I did. In my analysis and during these two days, I've been speaking about a very few cases where one can give explicit answers, exclusive answers. I'm talking about the degree of reliability, and I took such a view to look for something that can potentially be linked to Mr. Beara rather than what is not. What was possible, I then looked for a negative witness. For example, in court we have a witness that provides evidence, one, and the other one refutes that with his negative evidence. So this is the stance that I took within the framework of the corpus that I had at my disposal, and that was the best I could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to call it a day. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning, 9 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of August, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
